problems.stem: A quiz item responds to a wrong answer with only "Incorrect. Score: 0/1." Why is this not yet a feedback loop?
options: The score should be shown as a percentage instead of a fraction.
It delivers a verdict but no actionable information about what was misunderstood or what to try next.
It should award partial credit for effort.
The word Incorrect is too harsh and should be softened.
problems.explanation: A verdict alone closes nothing. A feedback loop tells the learner what was misunderstood and gives a next move, so the learner can act.

problems.stem: A module for first-week novices adds a "Skip any section" menu giving full freedom to reorder and exit. What is the design risk?
options: There is no risk; more control always improves motivation.
Novices often lack the prior knowledge to self-regulate, so unbounded skipping can let them miss the scaffolding they most need.
The menu will slow the page load.
Skipping is fine as long as a final exam blocks the exit.
problems.explanation: Learner control should be calibrated to expertise. Guided control, a recommended path with optional detours, suits novices better than unbounded freedom.

problems.stem: A vocabulary task is meant to build long-term retrieval. The designer attaches an instant answer reveal to every prompt. Why might delayed feedback serve this goal better?
options: Delayed feedback is cheaper to build.
For retrieval and self-monitoring tasks, a brief delay forces the learner to commit and self-assess first, which can strengthen retention more than an instant reveal.
Instant feedback is never appropriate in any task.
Delayed feedback prevents cheating, which is the main concern.
problems.explanation: Feedback timing is a design choice. Instant reveal can short-circuit the retrieval effort the task is built to produce.

problems.stem: Pilot data show 70 percent of learners who got the bare verdict "Incorrect" repeated the same error on the next attempt. Which revision is the strongest evidence-based response?
options: Add an encouraging emoji to the Incorrect message.
Replace the bare verdict with feedback that names the specific error type and offers one targeted retry, then re-pilot to see whether the repeat-error rate drops.
Lower the passing threshold so fewer learners see Incorrect.
Hide the score so learners feel less discouraged.
problems.explanation: The 70 percent repeat rate is evidence the loop is not closing. Actionable feedback plus a targeted retry, then re-measurement, is the defensible revision.
